title: Geoffrey Litt: Dynamic Documents as Personal Software
author: Geoffrey Litt
summary: Argues that apps are the wrong unit of personal software: an app is something someone else built to do one thing, whereas most real tasks are idiosyncratic enough that no app fits. The alternative is the document as a single flexible medium where data, computations and views mix freely, so people assemble the tool they need instead of adopting one. Litt traces this across eight years and three waypoints — Margin Notes for live programming, Embark for travel planning, and now Notion, where coding agents embed interactive HTML into ordinary docs. The lineage runs back to HyperCard, whose on-ramp pulled people from browsing to authoring to programming without ever showing a blinking cursor; the unofficial second title, 'how to take a rabbit hole very seriously', makes it equally a talk about sustaining one thread for years.
takeaways: Reading code is hard for a structural reason: computers run code on data, but you only see the code, so you end up simulating the data in your head. Live programming asks why the human is re-running what the machine already ran.

Margin Notes, his first project, let you click a method and see what it actually returned the last five times it ran, plus the object state at the time — 'more focused on understanding than correctness checking'.

Implementation was small: Ruby's TracePoint API hooks method calls and returns, dumps the interpreter's data structures to a file, and a UI renders them. He advises picking interpreted languages with this built in.
Recording the test suite instead of production sidesteps privacy and data-volume problems, and the test names become the example labels. Doing this on a currency library exposed a wrong docstring.
Embark, the travel-planning prototype, layers maps, weather, routing and a mini spreadsheet language into an ordinary note, chaining formulas (route distance → fuel cost → cost per person).

The first Embark prototype was a spatial canvas of linked widgets. It demoed well and failed in real use because there was nowhere to write down what you were thinking, which is what drove them back to the note.
Real trips stress-tested it: one collaborator planned an entire RV journey in it, another planned 'Poles of Inconvenience', a trip to deliberately awkward GPS points in Eastern Europe in a bad car.

He frames research as a ring diagram — good ideas people will pay for now (the startup zone) sit inside a wider ring of good ideas nobody will pay for yet. He left the outer ring for Notion because AI feels like a platform shift with a limited window.

Third waypoint is Notion: HTML blocks let a coding agent embed arbitrary interactive HTML in a doc while the surrounding text stays editable and commentable — deliberately better than one monolithic HTML page.

His 'explain diff' agent skill produces a literate diff: background first, intuition before detail, interactive figures (an adjustable isometric-tilt parameter), then a staged tour of the code with explanations at each step.
He appends a spaced-repetition quiz to each explainer and will not merge until he passes it — a deliberate speed regulator against rubber-stamping AI output you only think you understood.

Custom blocks (alpha) add shared database state so several blocks coordinate, which is what tips a document toward feeling like an app: org charts, milestone trackers, any vibe-coded UI over existing structured data.

Closing advice on sustaining a rabbit hole: optimise for interesting over legible or lucrative, find community to walk with, and treat organisational shape (startup, academia, independent lab, RC) as a design space rather than a given.
quotes: Computers run code on data, but you're only seeing the code. You're not seeing the data. And so, you're simulating data in your head.
On the right, you have apps, which are someone else made it to do one thing... every trip is weird and different in its own way.
None of what I'm showing you today is that new of an idea. It's all part of a lineage.

They had this on-ramp where they pulled you into programming, but you your starting point was not like a blinking cursor, your starting point was something that felt like a document to get you in the door.
As a medium books are surprisingly bad at conveying knowledge. And readers don't even realize it.
My rule personally is I have to pass the quiz before I merge the code, before I send it to someone else to review.

There's a big pile of good ideas out there waiting to be discovered, and only some of them are things that people will pay for right now... the point of research is to work in the outer circle to find the good ideas that people won't pay for now.
If the AI does it for you and you don't know how it did it, that may not achieve the full goal of you knowing what to build with it.
bestIdeas: The document as the unit of personal software, not the app. Where a task is genuinely idiosyncratic, a flexible medium beats any purpose-built tool — the test being whether an app for it could plausibly exist.
HyperCard's gradual on-ramp: browsing → authoring → programming, with no cliff. A design constraint for any system meant to grow non-programmers into builders, LifeOS included.
Show the data next to the code. Anchoring an abstraction in a handful of real past values is a general comprehension aid, and cheap wherever a runtime will expose its own internals.
Use the thing for real, early. Their best-demoing prototype failed on contact with an actual trip; speculation and use produce different designs.
The research ring — separating ideas people will pay for now from good ideas they won't yet — is a usable filter for deciding whether a piece of work wants a business or a lab around it.

Quiz-before-merge as an AI comprehension gate. Where it is easy to accept generated work you have not understood, an active-recall checkpoint converts passive reading into a pass/fail you cannot fool.

Keep the surrounding medium editable. Embedding a rich figure inside ordinary text beats rendering the whole artefact as one opaque document, because comments, edits and collaboration still work around it.
tools: Margin Notes — his live-programming prototype showing recorded return values and object state beside the source.
Ruby TracePoint — the interpreter API hooking method call/return events that made Margin Notes simple to build.
Embark — the dynamic-document travel planner: maps, weather, routing and an embedded spreadsheet language in a note.
HyperCard — the 1980s Apple system he cites as the lineage for the browse→author→program on-ramp.
Notion — where he now works, pursuing the same thesis commercially.
LIVE workshop — the live-programming academic venue where he first published the work.
Notion HTML blocks — launched feature letting a coding agent embed arbitrary interactive HTML in a doc; custom blocks with shared DB state are in alpha.
'Explain diff' — his own agent skill generating literate diffs with interactive figures and a closing quiz.
Riffle — his grad-school framework requiring all UI state to live in a synced multiplayer database.
method: Start from a document people already have, not a blank programming environment — Apple Notes, Notion or Obsidian are the intuition pump: 'how could this be more dynamic and more alive?'
Let data, computations and views mix freely in that one medium rather than splitting them across purpose-built apps.
Chain small formulas so outputs feed inputs (route → distance → fuel cost → per-person share).
Pull context from separate domains into one place so it can simply be compared side by side, e.g. an hourly forecast against a calendar event.
Use the prototype for real work, and let real friction — not demo appeal — drive the next version.
Design a gradual on-ramp: browsing, then authoring, then programming, so nobody faces a blinking cursor on day one.
For AI-generated code: teach background first, lead with intuition, add an interactive figure, then walk a staged literate diff — and close with a quiz you must pass before merging.

keyMessage: Personal software should start from a flexible document you already have rather than an app someone else designed, because the tasks worth automating are too idiosyncratic for anyone else to have built the right tool.
